confidence_why: Sheppard 2020 and the SIL Organised Phonology Data of 1992 both put default stress on the penultimate syllable with a leftward skip past a penult containing schwa (/ɨ/), and Anderson & Ross 2002 give plain penultimate stress, so the two independent descriptions of the Pamela dialect agree on placement and differ only on how fully predictable the exceptions are.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the penultimate syllable; when the penult contains schwa (orthographic ɨ) stress retracts to the antepenult; the author flags that stress is not fully predictable. The SIL OPD (Andersons 1992, p.5) independently states the same: stress probably not phonemic, usually penultimate, heavy syllables with a diphthong tend to attract stress, and stress shifts leftward off a syllable containing /ɨ/.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: Penult with schwa /ɨ/ -> antepenultimate stress (both sources); heavy (diphthong) syllables tend to be stressed (OPD); 'not always predictable' residue (both). Sheppard pp.133-134: in the verb complex, object indexes are never stressed, transitive/applicative =nga, =wana can be, and stem stress shifts depending on which bound morphemes are present.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a phonology overview; Sheppard separately describes clause intonation (declarative fall, polar-question rise on penult). Verb-complex clitic/affix stress behaviour treated as unresolved.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe Sudest as spoken on Vanatɨna (Sudest/Tagula) Island; the SIL OPD names Pamela village (Andersons' SIL base); Sheppard's fieldwork was on Vanatɨna and Yeina islands. Same languoid, sude1239; no dialect split relevant to the stress statement.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's penultimate placement (Sheppard 2020 p.51: 'frequently falls on the penultimate syllable (or the antepenultimate syllable, if the penultimate syllable contains a schwa)') and refines it: the OPD's leftward shift away from /ɨ/ is the same rule as Sheppard's schwa exception (the OPD writes the sixth vowel as /ɨ/), and the OPD adds that diphthong-heavy syllables attract stress, a weight effect not in the catalog. Both sources hedge that stress is not fully predictable; the OPD adds 'probably not phonemic'. Direct re-download from the sil. the p.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default penultimate stress, judged non-phonemic but not fully predictable; a diphthong-bearing (heavy) syllable attracts stress; a syllable containing the vowel /ɨ/ is skipped, stress moving one syllable leftward (so antepenultimate when the penult has /ɨ/).
new_statements.exceptions: Two stated deviations from the penultimate default: heavy diphthong syllables tend to attract stress; syllables with /ɨ/ repel it (stress shifts left). The section is headed 'tone, stress, length' but says nothing about tone; length is treated as contrastive vowel length in the vowel section (e.g. tu 'post' vs tuu 'yam type'), not as stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD (Andersons, Sept 1992) and the Anderson & Ross 2002 sketch describe the Pamela-village (south coast) dialect of Sudest/Tagula; Anderson & Ross note 'considerable dialect variation'. The OPD bibliography lists the grammar essentials ms as Anderson & Anderson 1992 (the target citation says 1991). Sheppard 2020 covers Sudest (Vanatɨna/Tagula) as sude1239/tgo; all sources are the same language.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction on placement: every source that speaks (SIL OPD 1992 p.5, Anderson & Ross 2002 p.323 via the on-disk excerpt, Sheppard 2020 p.51) puts default word stress on the penultimate syllable. The sources differ only on predictability: Anderson & Ross 2002 call stress 'predictable', whereas the OPD says 'probably not phonemic, but not always easily predictable either' and Sheppard says 'not always predictable'. The OPD and Sheppard agree on the /ɨ/ (schwa) skip; only the OPD mentions diphthong-heavy syllables attracting stress; only Sheppard discusses stress on bound verbal morphemes (object indexes never stressed, =nga and =wana can be; stem stress shifts with bound morphemes, pp.133-134). Anderson & Anderson 1991 itself could not be opened.
